label: Chapter 8: From Steel to Finance, and Luxembourg Today, 1980 to 2026

units.text: In the early 1980s, the steel industry that had built modern Luxembourg was shrinking.
Blast furnaces closed, and thousands of jobs vanished.
In many European industrial regions, this kind of decline led to decades of misery.
Luxembourg took a different path, and the reason was that a new industry was already growing in its shadow: banking and finance.
The seeds had been planted in the 1960s with the first Eurobond.
Over the following decades, the Grand Duchy built itself into a major international financial center.
Banks from around the world set up offices, attracted by its stability, its multilingual workforce, its flexible laws, and its famously strong banking secrecy.
In 1988, Luxembourg was the first country to write a 1985 European directive on cross-border investment funds into national law, which gave it a head start in that business.

Today, it is the largest center for investment funds in Europe, second in the world only to the United States, and the financial sector accounts for roughly a quarter of the whole economy by common estimates.
The old steel company went through its own transformation.
In 2002, ARBED merged with Spanish and French rivals to form a new company called Arcelor, which in 2006 was taken over by the steel group of the Indian-born businessman Lakshmi Mittal.
The result was ArcelorMittal, one of the largest steelmakers in the world, which is still headquartered in Luxembourg City.
And the old steel country found surprising new uses for its industrial heritage.
At Belval, in the far south near Esch, one of the biggest steelworks was shut down.
Its enormous blast furnaces were not demolished.

They were preserved as monuments, and around them rose a whole new district, with offices, a concert hall called the Rockhal, and the campus of the University of Luxembourg, which was founded only in 2003.
Where workers once tapped molten iron, students now study for exams.
At the same time, the country kept doing what it had done since the 1950s, which was to help build Europe.
In June 1985, on a passenger boat anchored on the Moselle river near the Luxembourg village of Schengen, five European countries signed an agreement to gradually abolish border checks among them.
Schengen is a tiny wine-growing village, where the borders of Luxembourg, France and Germany meet.
Its name is now known across Europe.
The Schengen Area, which allows millions of people to cross borders without passport control, was born on that boat.
Then came the greatest step toward integration: the euro.
In the early 1990s, as European leaders negotiated the Maastricht Treaty, which set the path to a single currency, Luxembourg's finance minister was a young politician named Jean-Claude Juncker.
He was a crafty, informal negotiator who helped broker the compromises that made the deal possible.
Juncker became prime minister in 1995 and held the job for eighteen years, longer than any other head of government in the European Union at the time.
He later chaired the group of eurozone finance ministers through the debt crisis, and in 2014, he was chosen as President of the European Commission.
He was not the first Luxembourger in that role.
Gaston Thorn led the Commission from 1981 to 1985, and Jacques Santer led it from 1995 to 1999.
Three presidents of the Commission, from one of the smallest countries in the union, is an extraordinary record.
It reflects what Luxembourg had always been good at: making deals among bigger partners, and making itself indispensable in the process.
Back at home, the language question was settled by law.
In 1984, Luxembourgish, the Moselle Franconian dialect that had been spoken at home for centuries, was formally recognized as the national language.
French and German remained the languages of law and administration.
Today, children in Luxembourg grow up with three languages in school, and many speak English, Portuguese, or Italian at home as well.
In few countries in the world is multilingualism such a normal part of daily life.
The country grew rich, and it grew crowded.
Today, Luxembourg has about two thirds of a million residents, and nearly half of them hold a foreign passport.
On top of that, around two hundred thousand people cross the border every day from France, Belgium and Germany to work.
Per head, the Grand Duchy has one of the highest standards of living in the world.
But it also has some of the highest housing costs in Europe, and the traffic jams on the roads into the capital are legendary.
In 2020, the government made all public transport free for everyone, the first country in the world to do so, partly as a way of easing the pressure.
The country has also looked to the sky.
A Luxembourg-based company, SES, launched the Astra satellites in the 1980s, which became one of the great satellite television success stories in Europe.
In 2017, the government passed a law on space resources, and in 2018, it created its own space agency, hoping to make Luxembourg a hub for the new space economy.
The modern era has not been free of controversy.
In 2008, Grand Duke Henri, who had come to the throne in 2000 on the abdication of his father Jean, announced that his conscience would not allow him to sign a bill legalizing euthanasia.
The government responded by changing the constitution, so that the Grand Duke would simply promulgate laws, rather than having to approve them.
It was a quiet constitutional change that further reduced the monarch's role in making laws.
And in 2014, a leak of confidential documents, known as LuxLeaks, revealed that Luxembourg had signed tax deals with hundreds of multinational companies, allowing them to pay very low taxes.
The outcry across Europe was fierce, and many officials in other countries said the Grand Duchy had been undermining its neighbors.

Luxembourg's government defended its legal framework but came under heavy pressure, and in 2015 it joined an international system for the automatic exchange of bank account information with other countries,
effectively ending the era of strict banking secrecy for foreign account holders.
The debate over what is fair in international taxation continues.
In politics, the stable Christian Social party dominated for most of the twentieth century.
From 2013 to 2023, a three-party coalition of liberals, Greens and social democrats governed under Prime Minister Xavier Bettel.
Then, in the election of October 2023, the Greens lost heavily, and the coalition lost its majority.
A new government took office in November 2023, led by Luc Frieden of the Christian Social party, in coalition with Bettel's Democratic Party.
Frieden is prime minister, and Bettel serves as deputy prime minister and foreign minister.
And there has been one more big moment, the most recent chapter of the oldest story.
On the twenty-third of June, 2025, Luxembourg's National Day, Grand Duke Henri announced that he would step down after twenty-five years on the throne.
On the third of October, 2025, in a ceremony at the Grand Ducal Palace, he formally abdicated in favor of his eldest son, Guillaume.

Guillaume, who was forty-three, swore an oath to the constitution before the country's parliament, and greeted crowds from a balcony of the palace, with his Belgian-born wife, Stéphanie, and their two young sons beside him.
He is the seventh grand duke of the modern line that began with Adolphe in 1890.
Voluntary abdication has become something of a tradition in this family, since Henri himself took the throne when his father stepped aside in 2000.
So let's step back and look at the whole journey.
It began in 963 with a count and a rock.
It passed through a golden age of emperors, who sat on the thrones of Prague, Budapest and Rome.
It became a fortress that foreign armies fought over for centuries, passed from Burgundy to Spain to France to Austria and back to France again.
It was created as a grand duchy in 1815, carved in half in 1839, saved from a war in 1867, occupied by Germany twice, and each time it recovered.
It turned from farms into steel, from steel into finance, and from a nation guarding itself into one of the founding pillars of a united Europe.
Through all of it, one thing has remained consistent.
The people of this small land, who have spoken three languages and lived under a dozen flags, have never stopped insisting on being themselves.
The line from that old song, written in the 1850s, still works as a national motto: Mir wëlle bleiwe wat mir sinn.
We want to remain what we are.
That is the story of Luxembourg.
Thank you for listening, and safe travels.
